uncited: Window-Closing Visibility Detection is a conservative visibility culling method designed for perspective navigation within large, tubular datasets, specifically virtual colonoscopy.

It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which subvolumes (represented as boxes) lie within the current viewing frustum without performing expensive per-box frustum intersection tests for all candidates.

It sets itself apart from its parent, the [Visible Zone Algorithm](9086-visible-zone-algorithm.md), by utilizing a 2D screen-space projection approach that iteratively shrinks a culling window, and from its sibling, the [Approximate Visibility Algorithm](13128-approximate-visibility-algorithm.md), by relying on the geometric "twisted" nature of the colon to guarantee that occlusion is handled via window degeneration rather than approximate distance bounds.
The algorithm operates on a preprocessed representation of the volume where the colon shape is approximated by a sequence of piecewise boxes.

It determines visibility by projecting these boxes onto the screen and maintaining an Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) that represents the visible portion of the screen through which subsequent boxes can be seen.
*   **Input:** A sequence of boxes $B_1, B_2, \dots, B_n$ approximating the colon, ordered by proximity to the viewer (or along the colon path).
The current camera view parameters (projection matrix, viewport).
*   **Current Cull Window (CCW):** A 2D axis-aligned bounding rectangle in screen space, defined by $(x_{min}, y_{min}, x_{max}, y_{max})$.
*   **Aggregate Cull Window (ACW):** A 2D axis-aligned bounding rectangle in screen space, initialized as the CCW of the first box and updated iteratively.
**Preprocessing:** Approximate the colon geometry with a sequence of piecewise boxes.
Order these boxes such that the algorithm begins with the closest box to the view point.
**Initialization:** Identify the first box $B_{start}$ closest to the view point.
**Project Initial Portal:** Project the vertices of the initial portal (the boundary of $B_{start}$ facing the viewer) onto the 2D screen plane.
**Compute Initial CCW:** Calculate the 2D axis-aligned bounding rectangle of the projected vertices.
This rectangle is the Current Cull Window (CCW) for the first box.
**Initialize ACW:** Set the Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) equal to the initial CCW.
The ACW represents the conservative bound of the visible area through the current box.
**Project Next Portal:** Project the vertices of $B_{next}$'s portal onto the screen.
**Compute Next CCW:** Calculate the 2D axis-aligned bounding rectangle of these projected vertices.
**Check Degeneration:** If the ACW is degenerate (i.e., $x_{min} \ge x_{max}$ or $y_{min} \ge y_{max}$, resulting in an empty or invalid area), stop the iteration.
The current box and all subsequent boxes are considered occluded or outside the visible frustum.
**Mark Visible:** If the ACW is valid, mark $B_{next}$ as visible and continue to the next box.
**Rendering:** Send all marked visible boxes to the volume rendering hardware for perspective rendering.
*   **Box Approximation:** The granularity of the piecewise box approximation affects accuracy and performance.
*   **Portal Definition:** The specific vertices used to define the "portal" of a box.
Typically the face of the box facing the camera or the interface between adjacent boxes.
*   **Degenerate ACW:** The algorithm relies on the ACW becoming empty to terminate.
If the colon geometry is not sufficiently "twisted" or occluded, the ACW may remain valid for many boxes, reducing culling efficiency.
*   **Perspective vs. Parallel:** The method is designed for perspective projection.
Incorrect ordering can lead to incorrect visibility determination.
*   **Time Complexity:** Linear with respect to the number of boxes until the ACW degenerates.
Each box requires projection and a constant-time rectangle intersection.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Constant space for the ACW and CCW, plus storage for the box sequence.
Avoids expensive 3D frustum intersection tests.
Performance degrades if the ACW does not degenerate quickly.
Limited to perspective projection as described.
*   **When to Use:** Interactive navigation in large, tubular volume datasets (e.g., virtual colonoscopy) where occlusion is frequent.
*   **When Not to Use:** Non-tubular structures, parallel projection, or scenes with low self-occlusion.
The Window-Closing Visibility Detection algorithm was developed for virtual colonoscopy applications to enable interactive navigation within large human colon datasets.
It was presented in the context of real-time volume rendering, leveraging the twisted nature of the colon to optimize visibility culling.
